newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan oil monopoly to privatise from mid-1997.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan oil monopoly to privatise from mid-1997.

text.p: Taiwan's state oil monopoly Chinese Petroleum Corp said on Thursday it would begin its long-awaited privatisation as early as July -- a half-year late -- and complete the process on schedule by July 2000.
"Chinese Petroleum will start the process in fiscal year 1997/98," company executive Liao Pei-feng told Reuters by telephone.
The monopoly's fiscal year starts on July 1.
Fifteen percent of company equity would be released in the first year to the local stock market to establish a market price for subsequent stock swaps with foreign oil companies, he said.
The process will be completed in fiscal year 1999/2000, when more than 50 percent of the company will be in private hands.
Vice president Roy Chiu has said the planned stock release would involve a public offering, stock swaps with oil-rich foreign states and sales to major investors.
"The stock swaps are intended to secure Taiwan's oil supply," Chiu told Reuters in a recent interview. "Any firm holding major oil reserves is a likely candidate for a swap."
Officials declined to give details or a timetable for the stock releases, swaps and other aspects of the privatisation.
The privatisation budget for fiscal 1997-98 still requires approval from what Liao called Taiwan's "unpredictable" parliament.
After months of delay, parliament adopted the monopoly's general 1996-97 budget on Thursday after further cuts in its investment projects.
Parliament had already cut the monopoly's fiscal 1996-97 privatisation budget during a June session after lawmakers demanded to re-evaluate the company's assets.
State regulators are requiring that Chinese Petroleum's selloff unfold gradually over three years to ensure that its massive capital requirements do not disrupt Taiwan's sensitive stock market.
"Taiwan's stock market would be hindered if we released Chinese Petroleum's stock all at once," Lai Tsai-fa of the state Commission of National Corporations told Reuters.
Based on the latest fiscal 1996 adjustment, the oil monopoly has a book value of over T$350 billion (US$12.7 billion) and T$230 billion (US$8.4 billion) in net assets.
Local media said the company's assets would likely surpass T$470 billion (US$17.1 billion) in a new assessment that is mandatory before the stock can be released.
Chinese Petroleum had planned to release 10 percent of its stock in 1996, but parliament froze the process for one year.

Company officials have warned such unexpected delays and possibly hasty reschedulings increased the risk of a disorderly privatisation that could result in control of the strategically important company falling into the hands of small but powerful interests, rather than the wider public as hoped.

The parliamentary freeze was led by ruling Nationalist Party lawmaker Chen Chao-jeng, who reasoned that he wanted to see the oil industry better regulated and Chinese Petroleum's assets more carefully evaluated before any equity was sold off.
Privatisation of Chinese Petroleum and other state giants aims to improve their competitiveness as Taiwan's economy liberalises and faces new global challenges.
Privatisation will also remove obstacles to the island's coveted entry to the free trade-championing World Trade Organisation.
